title: Recollecting generosity
hookLine: an old line that sounds backwards: it's a gain for me that I gave
tomorrow: are the gods in the old texts real beings, or a way of talking?

lines: HOW IS LETTING GO A GAIN?
cards: The card reader asks if you'd like to round up for charity, and there's a tiny pause before you tap yes or no. An old sutta has a line that sounds backwards in that pause.
Someone recalling a gift says, in effect: it's a gain for me, a real gain, that I gave. Not a gain for the person who got the gift. For me.
So here's the puzzle for today. How does something leaving your hands count as a gain?

teach.b: Read the whole line, and the puzzle starts to open. In the sutta the Buddha tells Mahanama how to recollect generosity.
It's a gain for me, a great gain, that in a world stained with stinginess I live with a mind free of that stain: open-handed, glad to let go, glad to share.
Now look at what's being counted. Not the object. The object is gone.
What's counted is the kind of mind that let it go. The gain is the open hand. The Pali word for generosity here is caga, a giving up, a letting go.
And nothing in the line measures the size of the gift. The Visuddhimagga, the meditation manual, solves the rest of the puzzle with something practical.

To remember giving, you have to have given. So the one who takes up this subject should be someone who keeps giving and sharing, and then goes over those gifts, gladly, the way yesterday went over conduct.
The same chain follows: a mind not taken over by greed, going straight, then gladness, calm, a settled heart.
Notice it's remembering, not scorekeeping. No ledger of who owes whom. Just a gift that left freely, and the hand that's still open.

how: Giving (dana) is part of daily Buddhist life: lay people offer food to monks, give to temples and to people in need, and Theravada teachers give the recollection of generosity as a meditation on gifts already given.

o: keeping a list of who owes you a favor
calling your own past gifts to mind, gladly
giving gifts only on holy festival days

games.q: what the line counts — tap the pairs.
p: a mind free of the stain of stinginess
be someone who gives and shares

s: recollecting generosity means planning your next good deed
it's remembering gifts that already left your hands, gladly.
in the sutta, the gain named is a mind free of stinginess
open-handed, glad to let go, glad to share: the open hand is what's counted.
the line says only big gifts are worth recalling
nothing in the line measures the size of the gift.

games.q: your little brother gave his favorite toy car to a cousin. now he's sad it's gone and asks if he did something dumb. what fits recollecting generosity?
o: remind him, gladly, that he's a kid who gives. that part stays.
buy him a new one, so the gift doesn't cost him anything.
tell him to stop thinking about it; it only makes it worse.
games.why: the toy is gone; the sutta never pretends otherwise. what it counts is the open hand, and remembering it gladly is the practice.

practice: On your fingers, count gifts you've given that left your hands freely: a ride, a hand-me-down, an hour on the phone, half a sandwich.
Stop wherever the count stops, then rest on the last one and let whatever gladness is in it spread a little.

wordCard.voice: Recollecting generosity: calling your own gifts to mind, gladly. The fifth recollection. The gain isn't the gift; it's the open hand that let it go.

orig.note: Pali: caga, giving up or generosity, with anussati, recollection.

carryVoice: Keep this one: glad of my giving, even the smallest gift you ever gave. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 6.10 (recollecting generosity: 'it is a gain for me' to live free of the stain of stinginess, open-handed, delighting in giving and sharing)
Visuddhimagga 7 (recollection of generosity, caganussati: the meditator should be devoted to giving and sharing)
